messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Teacher
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crowding: Crowded places, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Threat: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Callum is a 38-year-old high school history teacher of Scottish descent, married and living in a mid-sized American city. He presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after being mugged at knifepoint in a parking garage adjacent to a shopping centre on a Saturday afternoon. He had been returning to his car with his arms full of bags when two men closed in on him rapidly from either side, one pressing a blade against his ribs while the other rifled through his pockets and tore his watch from his wrist. The garage was crowded with weekend shoppers, and Callum remembers the specific smell of exhaust and damp concrete, the metallic taste of adrenaline flooding his mouth, and the sound of a car horn somewhere behind him that he initially mistook for a shout. No one intervened. He was left standing between two parked cars, shaking, as the men disappeared into the crowd. The police took a report, offered little, and the case was never pursued. Callum drove himself home that day, his wife in the passenger seat, neither of them knowing yet how completely that afternoon would reorganise his life.

In the weeks that followed, Callum found himself unable to stop the memory from returning without invitation. It would arrive without warning during lessons — the taste of that metallic flood suddenly present on his tongue, the full sensory weight of the moment reconstituting itself so completely that he would lose the thread of what he had been saying and have to grip the edge of his desk until the classroom reasserted itself around him. The intrusive quality of these recollections was not like ordinary remembering; they carried him back bodily, every sense engaged at once, the knife at his ribs as present as the whiteboard in front of him. When the memory surfaced, it reliably deepened his conviction that the world is a fundamentally dangerous place — a belief that had calcified quietly over months into something that now felt like simple fact rather than fear. And the memory, in returning, seemed to prime the very conditions that would summon it again: crowded spaces, the sensation of being hemmed in, the sound of a sudden loud noise in the corridor between classes — each of these could collapse the distance between then and now.

His classroom, once a comfortable domain, became a source of daily vigilance. Callum began arriving early to note where the exits were, positioning himself so that no student could approach from behind him unexpectedly. When a chair scraped suddenly across the floor or a door slammed, he would flinch and scan the room with an urgency he recognised as disproportionate but could not suppress. He had come to study the faces and body language of everyone who entered — students, colleagues, parents at open evenings — reading for signs of threat the way he once read historical documents for subtext. This hypervigilant scanning, far from reassuring him, kept returning him to the memory: the faces of the two men, the speed with which ordinary strangers had become dangerous, the crowd that had simply flowed around him as though nothing were happening. Each time he caught himself cataloguing exits or reading a stranger's posture for menace, it reinforced his certainty that the world warranted exactly this level of watchfulness, and that to relax it would be naive.

The sense of injustice ran deep and had not softened with time. Nothing had been done. The institution — the police, the system — had absorbed his report and returned nothing. Callum had come to believe that this outcome was not incidental but representative: that the world is dangerous and those charged with managing that danger are indifferent. These appraisals, when they surfaced, had a way of pulling the memory forward again, as though his mind were repeatedly returning to the evidence on which the verdict was based. Driving with his wife, who sometimes sat in the passenger seat exactly as she had on the day he drove home from the garage, had become nearly unbearable; the configuration alone was enough to trigger the full sensory return.

What finally brought Callum to seek help was a parent-teacher conference at which he had been so distracted by monitoring the room for threat that he could not recall a single conversation afterward. His wife had noticed the change in him long before he acknowledged it himself. He came to the intake session hoping, he said quietly, to be able to sit in a room without planning how to leave it.
